cq-options.description: A decision's alternatives, rendered as a card grid, for places where the reader picks one. Children are cq-option elements only. With `choose` (which requires an id), the reader picks a card — by click, or by keyboard via the toggle mark each card carries, which is also where its state reads. Clicking the picked card again clears it. The pick reaches Claude as a `choose` action naming the card, or null once cleared, and carries onto every later version by itself — marking the picked card `chosen` in the next version is how the record reads without the log, not what keeps the pick alive. A pick rests on the option picked, so rewriting what that option says needs its `restated` (see $restated in `catalog`); a pick the reader has cleared rests on the group, and takes the group's. `settled` (also requiring an id) retires a decision that has been made and acted on: the group collapses to one line naming the chosen option, with every card behind a disclosure the reader can open — the record keeps its ids and its anchors, and stops spending the page's height. Mark it once the choice has stopped being live, which is usually a version or two after honoring the pick, not the moment it was made; a settled group still takes a pick if the reader reopens it.
cq-options.x-example: Paper maps Print the route ahead of time; nothing to charge. Dedicated GPS Offline maps, week-long battery, reversible choice.

cq-option.description: One alternative in a decision. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. `recommended` draws the accent ring (the author's take); `chosen` the green one (the reader's pick — the choose upgrade sets it live, and the next version carries it so the page reads right without the log). `effort`/`risk` — the cost and the danger of picking this option — render as chips. Rewriting what a picked option says needs `restated` on that option (see $restated in `catalog`); the other options in the group are free to change.

cq-milestones.description: A timeline of milestones with status dots on a rail. Children are cq-milestone elements only.
cq-milestones.x-example: Survey the sites Map sun and squirrel routes. Build the feeders Two classic, two heated. Install and watch

cq-milestone.description: One milestone. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. `status` colors the timeline dot; `when` is a free-text schedule label; `tags` is a comma-separated list rendered as chips.

cq-timeline.description: A chronological event log — the incident-report shape. Children are cq-event elements only. Where cq-milestones tracks planned work by status, cq-timeline records what happened, when.
cq-timeline.x-example: Feeder camera offline Battery alert from the north feeder. Battery swapped Camera back Feed resumed.

cq-event.description: One event on a timeline. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. `at` is a free-text time label; `kind` colors the dot.

cq-compare.description: Labeled variants side by side — neutral exhibition, where cq-options is a decision. Children are cq-variant elements only.
cq-compare.x-example: Cedar Weathers silver; no sealant. Pine Cheaper; seal it yearly.

cq-variant.description: One variant in a comparison. Lead with a <strong> label; any content follows, widgets included.

cq-metrics.description: A KPI row. Children are cq-metric elements only.
cq-metrics.x-example:
<cq-metrics>
  <cq-metric id="k-visits" value="312" delta="+41" direction="up-good">daily visits</cq-metric>
  <cq-metric id="k-refills" value="2.1/wk" delta="+0.4" direction="up-bad">refills</cq-metric>
  <cq-metric id="k-species" value="14">species seen</cq-metric>
</cq-metrics>

cq-metric.description: One metric: element text is the label, `value` the headline number, `delta` a signed change (leading + or -), `direction` says which sign is good (up-good, up-bad) so the delta colors honestly; without it the delta stays neutral.

cq-ref.description: An inline reference to a source location, rendered as a link. `src` is path or path:line. The link base is resolved once per page from <meta name="cq-base" content="https://host/repo/blob/main/{path}#L{line}">; without that meta the reference renders as plain code.

cq-diff.description: A unified diff rendered with per-file collapse, add/del tints, and per-file +/− counts. The body is data: the diff verbatim, at column 0 (context lines keep their leading space), with < and > escaped as < and >. Comments anchor to the required id. Takes no language: each file's own path is read for one ($languages), so keep the `diff --git` or ---/+++ headers rather than pasting bare hunks, and a path naming no language leaves that file plain.
cq-diff.x-example:
<cq-diff id="mount-diff">
diff --git a/feeders/mount.py b/feeders/mount.py
--- a/feeders/mount.py
+++ b/feeders/mount.py
@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
 def bracket():
-    return "plastic"
+    return "steel"
</cq-diff>

cq-tree.description: A file tree from an indent-notation body: one node per line, children indented deeper, a trailing / marking a directory, trailing +N/-N tokens rendering as change badges. Body is data — text only.
cq-tree.x-example:
<cq-tree id="feeder-tree">
feeders/
  mount.py  +2 -2
  schedule.py  +1
  sites/
    north.toml
</cq-tree>

cq-code.description: An annotated code block — the walkthrough shape. The body is the code verbatim (data, < and > escaped, column 0); `lang` colors it; `hi` highlights line ranges ("3-5,8"); cq-note children anchor remarks at lines. Leave `lang` off where the body isn't source (a transcript, command output) — nothing guesses, so an undeclared block stays plain.
cq-code.x-example:
<cq-code id="bracket-walk" lang="python" hi="2">
def bracket(temp):
    if temp < 0:
        return "steel"
    return "cedar"
<cq-note at="2">Freezing is the only threshold that matters.</cq-note>
</cq-code>

cq-note.description: A remark anchored at a line of its cq-code parent. Prose content; `at` is the 1-based line number.

cq-diagram.description: A diagram rendered from a mermaid-source body (flowchart, sequence, state…). The body is data, not prose: text only, angle brackets escaped as < and >. Comments anchor to the required id, not to text inside the SVG.
cq-diagram.x-example:
<cq-diagram id="checkout-flow">
graph LR
  Cart --> Pay
  Pay --> Receipt
</cq-diagram>

cq-shot.description: A before/after pair of screenshots of one view, shown one at a time in a single frame: the reader clicks between them and the change is the only thing on screen that moves. `before` and `after` are served image paths — `colloquy media <dir> <file>…` copies files into the page directory and prints the path to write, which is the only way an image gets onto a page (a screenshot is far too many bytes to inline). `alt` says what the pair shows, for a reader who can't see it. The element takes no content: what the page has to say about the change is ordinary prose written around it, where the reviewer can quote it. Reach for it when the change reads at page scale — layout, spacing, a component swapped out. Below that scale the column's width is against you: crop the pair to the part that moved, or show the element itself before and after at real size.
cq-shot.x-example:
The option cards

Effort and risk now sit above the title, so a scanning eye reads cost before prose.

cq-board.description: A kanban board the reviewer edits directly: cards move between columns or reorder within one — dragged by the grip, or by keyboard (the grip is a button: Enter grabs, arrows move, Enter drops) — and each completed move reaches Claude as a `move` action naming the card, target column, and position. Children are cq-column elements only. Write the board as you mean it and leave it alone afterwards: a recorded move carries onto every later version by itself, so re-emitting a card where you first put it does not undo the reviewer's move. A move rests on its card, so revising one they have moved is the card's `restated` (see $restated in `catalog`), never the board's.
cq-board.x-example: Heated perch Wire the south feeder. Squirrel baffle Camera mount

cq-column.description: One column on a board. `label` is the column heading, and the name a screen reader announces for the list of cards beneath it — so it has to read as the column's name on its own. Children are cq-card elements only; an empty column is a valid drop target.

cq-card.description: One card on a board. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. The reviewer drags it by its grip; the id names it in `move` actions and keeps comment anchors stable across moves. Rewriting a card the reviewer has moved needs `restated` on the card (see $restated in `catalog`), which retracts the moves of that card alone — the rest of the board keeps its arrangement.

cq-tabs.description: Parallel workstreams on one page: each cq-tab child is a self-contained sub-context (its own prose, boards, milestones) and a generated strip switches between them. The open tab is the reader's view state — remembered per browser tab like scroll position, never an action, never carried by a version — and the first panel is the default, so ordering carries emphasis. Find-in-page and comment-anchor jumps reach inactive tabs (the owning tab opens itself). Children are cq-tab elements only; unupgraded, panels stack as labeled sections.
cq-tabs.x-example:
Rebuild underway; two of four feeders mounted.

Heater options under review.

cq-tab.description: One workstream panel. `label` names its tab in the strip (and the stacked heading before upgrade); content is open — prose, sections, and other widgets nest freely. Ids inside share the page's one universe, so keep them distinct across tabs.

cq-suggestion.description: One proposed change to content the reviewer has already seen, decided in place. cq-old holds the current markup verbatim, cq-new the proposal: both slots replace, cq-new alone inserts, cq-old alone deletes. Pending, the old reads struck and the new tinted, with accept/reject controls in the page margin; deciding collapses the element to the settled markup and reaches Claude as an `accept` or `reject` action for the next version to carry. `resolves` names the comment whose thread this change answers — accepting resolves that thread too. Suggestions don't nest, and a reply can't carry one (reply markup is frozen in the log, so no version could settle it). Fresh content — a new section, the first version — is written straight instead, and a block the reviewer is to write in their own words is a cq-draft: theirs to rewrite, not Claude's to propose. The reviewer can also just comment on a pending suggestion rather than decide it.
cq-suggestion.x-example:
Refill rules for the season:

Refill every feeder each morning.

Refill a feeder when its camera shows it half-empty.

cq-old.description: The markup a suggestion would replace or delete, verbatim — ids and all, which live here while the suggestion is pending. Omitted when the suggestion only inserts. Accepting the suggestion retires this slot: its words leave the page's reading, so nothing can anchor on them after.

cq-new.description: The markup a suggestion proposes. Omitted when the suggestion only deletes. Rejecting the suggestion retires this slot: its words leave the page's reading, so nothing can anchor on them after.

cq-draft.description: A block of text the reviewer owns: they double-click it (or its ✎ button) to rewrite it in place, and the exact words reach Claude as an `edit` action naming the element. The body is the draft text verbatim (data, < and > escaped; newlines preserved). It carries no decision chrome of its own — put a draft inside a cq-card where the column is the verdict, or let page sign-off close the review. Usable anywhere prose flows. Claude rewriting prose of its own goes in a cq-suggestion instead; a draft is the reviewer's own words, so there is nothing for them to accept. Once they have edited one those words are theirs: re-emit the body you wrote and their edit still stands over it — and `comment` reads it their way, quoting the words their edit left and refusing the ones it replaced. To take the pen back — a fact of yours to fix in a sentence they rewrote — write the new text and mark the element `restated` (see $restated in `catalog`).
cq-draft.x-example:
<cq-draft id="note-cli">
Adds --dry-run to every mutating command.
</cq-draft>

cq-specimen.description: Quoted material: a region the page exhibits rather than speaks — a sample decision, a demo board, markup shown as an example. Renders as quotation: a hairline left gutter under a small-caps "specimen" line (`label` extends it — "specimen · a decision"). Content is open and renders at full fidelity, but it is a mention, not a use: interactive widgets inside are inert — a choose group takes no clicks, a board no drags, a suggestion no decision. Keep the content visibly fictional, and let the gutter do the marking: a caption explaining that the region is an example is the page narrating a widget it could just use.
cq-specimen.x-example: Paper maps Nothing to charge. Dedicated GPS Offline maps, week-long battery.

$languages.description: The languages this page's layer can color, and what a filename means. `names` is the whole vocabulary: what an author may declare, what the lint refuses a word outside, and what scripts/vendor-highlight.sh builds the tokenizer bundle from. It is a property of the page rather than of any widget, which is why it lives here and not under the schema of whichever tag happens to take a `lang` — a widget declares that one of its attributes names a language (x-language) and the lint reads the list from here, so a second tag taking one costs a declaration and no new reader. `paths` is the half nobody writes: the one place a language is derived rather than declared, because a unified diff spans files and so has no attribute to carry one. An extension is the diff's own statement about what a file holds, which is a declaration like any other; an extension absent here leaves that file plain.
$languages.why-diff-is-not-a-path: `diff` is in `names` and deliberately not in `paths`: a .patch inside a diff would be colored by the diff grammar, whose addition and deletion ink is the same statement the widget's own tints already make — said twice, in two channels, about the same line.

$events.description: The vocabulary stamp: the event kinds this layer's runtime and CLI read, and the fields each carries beyond id/ts/author/kind/seq. Vendored with the page, it is the one statement of what that page's runtime speaks — `note` refuses to write a shape the page's vendored copy doesn't declare (an old runtime drops unknown shapes silently), and `init` refuses to re-vendor over a log recorded in kinds or verbs (x-state, per widget) the incoming layer no longer speaks, because those events would never replay again. A registry with no $events predates the stamp and is read as exactly the pre-stamp vocabulary.

$state.description: What x-state declares, once per widget with an action channel: each verb's detail schema (the payload half of the log's forever-contract), its fold unit, and the record form its state takes in markup. Every applyAction is absolute, so the reviewer's standing state is a fold — the last surviving action per unit — and one declaration drives four readers: `check`'s state gate (a version whose markup actively contradicts the fold without `restated` is refused; writing the folded state is honoring; re-emitting the previous version's state is blessed silence), the record-lag report, the runtime's decided-but-unhonored mark, and the version diff's state half.
$state.unit: "widget" for a verb absolute across the group (choose toggles every sibling), or the detail field naming the element the verb is absolute per (move's "card").
$state.record: How the state reads in markup: {kind: "attribute", attr, value} — the element inside the unit carrying attr, vs the detail field `value`; {kind: "position", within, value} — the enclosing `within` element, compared at that granularity (indexes compose across cards, so column is the whole comparison); {kind: "body", value} — the unit's own words. A verb with no record (accept/reject) folds for the runtime's pending mark, and retirement stays retirable_ids' business.

$restated.description: A boolean attribute saying this version has rewritten words a reviewer already decided on, so what they decided no longer applies and they are being asked again. It goes on the element the decision rests on — a cq-draft or cq-suggestion, or the cq-card or cq-option inside a board or group — and retracts what rested on that element alone: one rewritten card drops the moves of that card, leaving the rest of the board arranged as the reviewer left it.
$restated.why: A move, pick, edit or accept is recorded in the log against the version it was made on, and the page replays every recorded action onto every later version. A decision therefore survives a republish on its own — you never carry one into the next version's markup, and re-emitting a widget as you first wrote it does not undo it. The cost is that your markup cannot quietly overrule them either, which is what this attribute is for.
$restated.when: Only where a later version has to change what the reviewer decided about: an error you found in a draft they rewrote, a picked option whose prose was wrong. Write the new words, mark that element, and say why in the note — to the reviewer this reads as a decision undone, and the note is where a version explains itself. `check` refuses a version that changes those words without it and a `restated` that retracts nothing, so it can be neither forgotten nor spent as a reflex; when it names the wrong element, the error says which one it wanted.
$restated.once: It belongs to the one version that does the rewriting. Publishing records the retraction in the log, so it holds for good — later versions leave the attribute off, and `check` refuses one that repeats it.
$restated.example:
<cq-draft id="note-cli" restated>
Adds --dry-run to every mutating command. It defaults on for `purge`.
</cq-draft>

$idioms.description: Recurring shapes the theme styles directly — no registry entry, no JS. Plain semantic HTML gets the theme's voice for free; these classes cover what HTML lacks an element for.

.eyebrow.description: A small-caps label above a heading.

.lede.description: The opening paragraph, set slightly larger.
.lede.example: One paragraph saying what this page decides.

.callout.description: An aside set off from the prose — a tinted field with a hairline border.
.callout.example: <aside class="callout">Rollback is one flag flip; the backfill is idempotent.</aside>

.facts.description: A label/value grid for summary facts, as a definition list.

ol.steps.description: An ordered procedure with numbered markers.
ol.steps.example:
1. Backfill the new store.
  2. Verify counts, then flip reads.

details.description: Evidence: a claim as the <summary>, its backing collapsed beneath. Native disclosure; find-in-page reaches the collapsed content.
details.example:
The parser drops the slash on self-closed custom tags 
document.querySelector("cq-ref").textContent
// → "rest of the paragraph"

pre > code.language-*.description: A literal the reviewer can select and quote: a command to run, a config file, a snippet of output. Name the language to color it — the same set cq-code's `lang` takes, and `check` refuses one outside it. Leave the class off where the body isn't source; nothing is guessed from the text. Reach for cq-code instead when the block is a walkthrough: numbered lines, highlighted ranges, remarks anchored at a line.
